summary:
We built Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a free web app that shows, in seconds, whether a lunar landing site will see the Sun (power) and Earth (direct communication) on any chosen date, and for how long.

Users pick up to four sites (Apollo, Chandrayaan-3, NASA CLPS landers, Chang'e, SLIM, or any coordinates) and a landing date. The app traces each site's real skyline from NASA's LRO laser-altimeter (LOLA) terrain and moves the Sun and Earth across it using JPL's planetary ephemeris. It reports the time until sunset and Earthset, sunlight and Earth visibility, solar power, the battery needed for the longest night, the best landing dates if a launch slips, and how results change if the lander moves a few hundred metres.

This matters most at the south pole, where the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon and a single hill can decide a mission. Results are validated against JPL Horizons and NASA's own LOLA sunlight maps.
details:
What it does
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web app that answers a mission planner's first questions about a landing site: will the lander see the Sun (power) and Earth (direct-to-Earth communication), and for how long? Users pick up to four sites and a landing date. They can choose from 16 curated sites (Apollo 11–17, IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Blue Ghost 1, Chang'e 4/5/6, a ridge near Shackleton crater, Shackleton's shadowed floor) or enter any coordinates. The app shows:

  • whether the Sun and Earth are up, and the time until sunset/Earthset (or sunrise/Earthrise)
  • a comparison table: sunlight %, Earth visibility %, both together, mean solar power, longest darkness, the battery needed to survive it, and the longest radio silence
  • a sky view: the real skyline with the Sun's and Earth's paths over it
  • a 3D terrain view with a time slider
  • a timeline of power and maximum downlink rate
  • "Best landing dates": sunlight and Earth contact for every landing day over the next year, for any mission length
  • "Move the site": a 9×9 grid showing how results change a few hundred metres away

How it works

  1. Sun and Earth directions come from JPL's DE440 planetary ephemeris and the Moon's orientation, including libration, via NASA NAIF SPICE. They're rotated into local east/north/up axes at the site.
  2. The skyline is found by tracing rays outward in 720 directions over NASA LRO LOLA laser-altimeter terrain: 40 m pixels near the south pole, 474 m elsewhere. It's done in 3D, so the Moon's curvature is included.
  3. The Sun counts as visible when any part of its disc is above the skyline, and power scales with the visible part. Radio contact needs Earth's centre above the skyline.
  4. Power is sunlight (1361 W/m², adjusted for distance) × panel area × efficiency × panel angle. Radio uses a standard X-band link budget. Panel, radio and mast-height values are editable assumptions.

Validation

  • Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons to 0.006 arcseconds (52,560 comparisons).
  • Sunlight and Earth-visibility percentages agree with the NASA LOLA team's 18.6-year south-pole maps (Mazarico et al.) to a median of 0.5 and 0.1 percentage points over 142 sites.
  • For Chandrayaan-3, the tool gives sunrise on 21 August and sunset on 4 September 2023, the lunar day ISRO operated in.

Benefits and intended impact
When a launch slips or a site changes, planners can compare alternatives in minutes instead of working through several specialist tools. Example: at the IM-2 site, a 14-day mission landing on 7 November 2026 gets 45% sunlight, but landing on 15 November gets 100% Sun and Earth contact. For teachers and the public, the sky and 3D views show why the south pole is so hard: the Sun never rises more than about 1.5°, so a single hill can decide a mission.

What's creative about it

  • It turns raw ephemeris and terrain data into answers a planner can act on ("rises in 7 days"; "land 8 days later for 100% sunlight") rather than raw angles.
  • The "best landing dates" scan and the "move the site" grid make the sensitivity to date and location visible, which the challenge specifically asks about.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: each part is checked against an independent NASA source.
  • Partial Sun: a half-hidden Sun gives half the power.
  • Mast height: at the pole even 1 m changes the answer, so it's a slider.
  • Earth's wobble: the Moon's libration moves Earth up and down in the sky by about 7° every month.
  • Curvature: the Moon's curvature affects distant terrain.
  • Speed and accessibility: the online version uses an 80 MB terrain set that matches the full 1.1 GB version within 0.06 percentage points at the curated sites. The app also runs offline on a laptop.

Tools
Python, SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF SPICE toolkit), NumPy, pandas, Streamlit, Plotly and Matplotlib. Hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. Code:https://github.com/anna-vaz/lunar-landing-site-navigator
